newsitem.title: FRANCE: More protests planned over French immigrant bill.
newsitem.headline: More protests planned over French immigrant bill.

text.p: Opponents of a controversial French bill to clamp down on illegal immigrants have urged new street protests after the National Assembly approved the measure and sent it to the Senate for a final reading.

A coalition of anti-racism groups called for a mass demonstration on March 9, two days before the Senate begins its debate on the centre-right government's move to close loopholes in tough existing laws dating from 1993 and to grant police extended powers to track immigrants in France.

"Behind the pretext of this 'battle against illegal immigration', the real intent is to undermine the process of integrating immigrants living in France," said a coalition statement after Thursday's 113-61 National Assembly vote.
"The entirety of this law is dangerous," said the statement.

It added that the new protest march was intended to pressure the conservative government to withdraw the bill and replace it with "positive measures based on the recognition of fundamental rights and liberties".
The bill was passed by the assembly on the third day of often acrimonious debate.
Leftist deputies urged the government to drop the bill after artists and intellectuals launched petition drives and took to the streets to denounce the measure in a series of protest marches.

A protest on Saturday drew around 100,000 peaceful demonstrators but a second march on Tuesday night turned violent when riot police clashed with marchers throwing rocks at them. Thirty police officers were injured.
The bill has triggered a broad, emotional debate in France on racism and xenophobia at a time of a near-record jobless rate of 12.7 percent, soaring social welfare costs and rising violent crime.
The government says the bill is necessary to close loopholes in the current law.

It has also portrayed the measure as a way to improve the employment situation and to discourage citizens of Third World countries who might be considering sneaking into France to take advantage of its generous welfare benefits.
But opponents accuse the government of pandering to the growing number of voters supporting the extreme-right National Front. They say the government has its eye on the 1998 general election.
The critics say the measure will encourage French citizens to develop racial hatreds and to fear foreigners.
Socialist leader Lionel Jospin has pledged to do away with the bill if his party wins the general election due in March next year.
